fields.title: Five Typical Paths
fields.keyTakeaway: Most leaks happen through compromised access, open storage, and permission check errors, and the product area of responsibility is the latter plus deciding what data even exists.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: How do data leaks happen most often — hacking or something else?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: Viewing a leak as a hacker attack leads to defending against the wrong things. Most real leaks happen more simply, and some of the paths are created by product decisions.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: Five paths, in order of frequency.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: **Compromised employee access.** Stolen password, phishing, [[social-engineering|social engineering]]. The most frequent path. Two-factor authentication for employees closes most of it.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: **Exposed storage.** A backup, log storage, test database accessible without a password due to a configuration error. Discovered by scanners in hours.
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: **[[excessive-privileges|Excessive privileges]].** An employee or service has broader access than necessary. A leak happens not because someone is malicious, but because a compromised account opens more than it should.
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: **Through the product.** An error in permission checks: a parameter in a request allows getting someone else's data. A separate case is a cache without a user identifier, as in `SC1-N4-L1`.
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: **Through third parties.** A contractor, integration, analytics service. Data leaks on their side.
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: What of this is the product manager's domain:
fields.sections/2/blocks/7/text: *Through the product* — directly: permission checks on every operation, cache keys, request parameters. *Excessive privileges* — directly: the permissions model from `SE1-N1-L2`. *Through third parties* — directly: deciding who to transfer what data to.
fields.sections/2/blocks/8/text: And a general lever: **minimization.** Data that does not exist cannot leak. Data that is not transferred to a contractor cannot leak at the contractor's end.
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: Three cases in two years, all non-hacker incidents.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: *Cache without an identifier.* The feed was cached without tying it to the user, and some people saw someone else's feed. 40 minutes, dozens of people. A product error.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: *Test database with real data.* A production copy for debugging on a server without access restrictions. Discovered ourselves during an audit. Since then — only anonymized data in test environments, with automatic anonymization upon copying.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: *Analytics service.* Full delivery addresses were going into event tracking. Not a leak, but a transfer to a third party without a legal basis. Removed, left only the city.
fields.sections/3/blocks/4/text: Rule after the third case: **the list of fields going to external services is checked on every event change.** Automated check: if a field from the black list appears in an event, the build fails.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: It is impossible to completely eliminate leaks. The goal is to close frequent paths and limit the volume of potential damage through minimization.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: Most leaks happen through compromised access, open storage, and permission check errors, and the product area of responsibility is the latter plus deciding what data even exists.
